context.clinical_context_summary: 79-year-old female with extensive past medical history including severe sepsis with septic shock, chronic respiratory failure with hypercapnia, COPD, atrial fibrillation, cardiomyopathy, prediabetes, hypertension with current hypotension, acute kidney failure, Brown-Sequard syndrome (spinal cord disease), and OSA, on anticoagulants, atorvastatin, vitamin C, and calcium-vitamin D. Presents with BLOOD INFECTION (likely recurrent sepsis given history). HIGH-RISK PATIENT: History of septic shock, chronic respiratory failure, and cardiac compromise significantly increase mortality risk. Temperature readings (mean 34.72°C, range 33.2-35.7°C) suggest axillary/peripheral measurement; hypothermia in sepsis is a grave prognostic sign and should not be dismissed. Baseline hypotension (SBP mean 80, DBP mean 48) reflects chronic cardiovascular compromise; even modest drops may indicate decompensation.
context.rationale: Thresholds are personalized based on this high-acuity patient's chronic conditions: (1) HR upper limit extended to 100 bpm due to atrial fibrillation and sepsis-related tachycardia risk; lower limit conservative given cardiac history. (2) BP thresholds accommodate baseline hypotension (SBP mean 80, DBP 48); critical threshold set at SBP <60 given septic shock history. (3) SpO2 normal floor set at 88% due to COPD with chronic hypercapnia (permissive hypoxemia); warning at 85% given respiratory failure history. (4) RR upper normal extended to 22 bpm reflecting her baseline with chronic respiratory failure. (5) Temperature thresholds adjusted for apparent axillary measurement (mean 34.72°C); hypothermia <33.5°C or fever >38.5°C in sepsis context warrants immediate attention, as hypothermic sepsis carries worse prognosis than febrile sepsis.
